title: The Value of Retreating Moves | Sicilian Defense | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: The bishop to c4 right away — essentially playing the Italian against the Sicilian, which is pretty innocuous.
The bishop wants to make contact with f7, but once we can play e6 and shut it out, the move makes very little sense.
No need to play e6 right away — White isn't threatening to take on f7 — so first bring the knight out.
a3 is probably not real preparation — and the best answer to odd play is to follow principles to a tee.
The simplest approach: the other knight to f6. And White can't play e5, because that square is defended — that's exactly why we played the knight to c6 first.
The centre fork trick — take on e4, then win the piece back with d5 — is available, but here it's a little premature and leads to needless complications.
Simpler is e6, preparing to expand with d5 — and the fork-trick idea doesn't disappear, it just depends on how White develops.
The bishop retreats to a2 — no more fork trick, but we simply keep calmly expanding in the centre.
Playing principled chess against a second-string opening — d5, grabbing the centre and taking it right to the opponent.
Recapture with the pawn — already a very pleasant position, with the better control of the centre.
Develop the kingside, since our king is still in the centre — but note White signals d4, and we mustn't sleepwalk into an isolated-queen-pawn structure with that bishop eyeing d5.
